ARKD: The ARK Innovation ETF wrapped in a buffer for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the first quarter, softening part of any loss in that volatile growth fund while capping gains. The defense is the point: it trades some upside for a cushion under a fund famous for big swings.
ATC: Autocallable notes tied to a single stock, Coinbase, the crypto exchange, structured to pay income and potentially end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with fine print: everything rides on one crypto-linked stock whose price already swings with the whole crypto market.
AUGC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. The August start fixes the terms: this edition's shallower buffer leaves a higher cap than deeper-protection versions.
BFJA: Bitcoin exposure with a built-in floor, using options to limit losses over an outcome period that started in January while keeping some upside. It is a cautious way to hold a volatile asset: the floor softens drops, gains are capped, and the terms reset each period.
CAUG: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. The late-summer start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CSEP: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. The autumn start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CTAU: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection costs upside: the cap is low, so it trails badly in strong rallies.
CTSE: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection costs upside: the cap is low, so strong rallies mostly pass it by.
CWY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to CoreWeave, the AI data-center company. It stacks options on leverage on one young, volatile stock at the center of the AI buildout, so payouts can be large but swings are extreme and holding periods should be short.
DCAP: Preferred shares issued by bitcoin treasury companies, the firms that hold bitcoin as their main asset, plus derivatives on those shares, all aimed at current income. It is crypto income at one remove: payouts depend on bitcoin-rich balance sheets, so bitcoin's swings drive everything.
EMAU: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, and gains capped in exchange. It adds late-summer defense to developing markets, where political and currency swings are part of the ride.
EMJL: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, and gains capped in exchange. It adds mid-year defense to developing markets, where political and currency swings are part of the ride.
EMJN: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, and gains capped in exchange. It adds mid-year defense to a volatile asset class: EM and currency swings still show through.
EMSE: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, and gains capped in exchange. It adds autumn defense to developing markets, though their political and currency swings still show through.
EXEQ: The 50 large US companies scoring highest on a leadership ranking that grades management quality and execution, spread across industrials, energy, health care and consumer stocks. It is a core holding with a management filter: the bet is that well-run companies win, whoever measures it.
GLBL: Large companies worldwide, tilted toward whichever industries are strongest in each country compared with a global benchmark, led by technology. It is a core global holding with an industry twist: the country-by-country industry bets set it apart from a plain world index fund.
HSEP: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the defensive extreme of its series: the autumn start fixes the terms, and the cap is tight.
IDSE: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It pairs foreign exposure with autumn defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
INDQ: Indian companies screened for quality: the profitable, well-run firms of the subcontinent, spread across consumer, health care, industrial and financial names. It is an actively selected single-country growth bet: India's young consumer economy drives it, with currency and political swings on top.
KDRN: A fund of bond funds, shifted tactically among mortgage bonds, short-term Treasuries and high yield debt, including a slice of CCC rated bonds, the riskiest tier of junk. It is a flexible income holding: the manager's calls on rates and credit decide how it does.
MCOW: Mid-sized US companies with at least seven straight years of positive free cash flow and strong cash returns, led by technology and industrials. It is a quality screen on the market's middle tier: the long cash-flow record is the filter, favoring proven mid-caps over speculative growers.
MEMY: Stocks that social media has turned into memes, the heavily hyped names retail traders pile into, paired with an options strategy for income. It is a deliberately speculative income trade: the underlying stocks swing on buzz rather than business results, so payouts and prices are both unstable.
MHIG: Mostly Treasury bonds and short-term Treasury funds, with small slices of health care stocks, broad stocks and gold, all aimed at keeping pace with rising medical costs. It is a cautious niche hedge: defense comes first, so it will not race ahead when markets boom.
PBCS: Consumer staples companies from around the world: the food, drink, household goods and personal care makers people buy in good times and bad. It is a defensive sector building block: staples are famous for steadiness, and the global spread adds currency swings to an otherwise calm holding.
PBUB: US banks of all sizes, from giant money-center lenders to regional banks, and nothing else. It is a pure sector building block: the whole fund rises and falls with bank profits, interest rates and credit quality, with no other industries to soften a banking slump.
PIEL: Giant companies outside the United States chosen for how much they sell abroad: chipmakers, drug makers, luxury brands and food giants that lead world trade. It is a foreign growth holding, so it rides global demand, and a strong dollar or trade slowdown hits it directly.
PTNT: Companies that earn money from intellectual property: patent holders, brand owners and entertainment firms paid royalties when others use their ideas, characters and inventions. It is a global bet on owning the rights rather than the factories, so income depends on licensing deals and legal protection holding up.
QJN: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It is tech growth with a mid-year safety net: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains than deeper versions.
QQBF: Nasdaq-100 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over each quarterly outcome period, with gains capped in exchange. The quarterly reset sets it apart from year-long buffers: protection terms refresh four times a year, so timing matters less.
QQQB: Nasdaq-100 exposure with an options shield designed to protect more of the downside than a typical buffer, while keeping a share of the upside. It is tech growth with armor: the shield softens drops in a volatile index, paid for by giving up part of strong rallies.
QQSE: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It blends tech growth with autumn defense: gains are capped, and the September start fixes the protection terms.
RB: Small US companies with an options buffer that resets daily, using one-day options to soften losses whenever the small-cap market falls. Unlike year-long buffer funds, its cushion is rebuilt every day, so protection is always fresh but never promised for any set period.
REAI: Real estate companies led by data center owners, with industrial warehouses, self-storage sites and cell towers behind them, picked by Armada's models rather than by hand. It is a property income holding with a tech flavor: data centers tie its fortunes to cloud and AI demand.
SCJL: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It adds mid-year defense to smaller stocks: gains are capped, and the July start fixes how much protection remains.
SCJN: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It adds mid-year defense to the market's jumpiest tier: the buffer helps, but small-cap swings and the gain cap both bind.
SCSE: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It adds autumn defense to the market's most volatile tier: small-caps swing hard, so the buffer does real work here.
SLVY: Exposure to silver through funds and income-producing investments, aiming to pay a target level of income while following the metal's price. It blends a commodity bet with payouts: silver swings harder than gold, and the income layer trades some of that movement for steadier cash.
TMH: One company, Toyota, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge that removes most of the yen-to-dollar exchange rate effect. It is a single-stock bet on the world's biggest carmaker with currency swings stripped out, so the result follows the car business alone.
TROT: US Treasury bonds with a twist: the fund rotates between longer and shorter maturities to adjust how hard interest-rate moves hit it. It is an actively timed government bond holding: when the rotation is right it cushions rate rises, and when wrong it adds swings a plain Treasury fund avoids.
TTOP: The ten largest crypto assets globally: bitcoin, ether and the next biggest networks, reached through regulated instruments rather than direct holdings. It is the whole top of the crypto market in one fund: bitcoin dominates the weight, and the smaller coins add extra swing.
VAIC: Autocallable notes tied to a basket of 500 large US stocks, using a conservative version of the structure that pays income and can end early. It is structured income with a cautious setting: returns depend on the notes' terms and the market staying above set levels, not on owning the stocks.
VOOB: S&P 500 exposure with an options shield designed to protect more of the downside than a typical buffer, while keeping a share of the upside. It is a defensive core holding from a newer family of protection funds: the shield's exact terms, set by its options, decide how it behaves in a crash.
WDAI: The 300 largest companies from stock markets around the world, chosen with an AI-driven scoring approach, in one global growth portfolio. It is a broad core holding with a machine-made selection: the AI screen decides the leaders, but the fund still moves with world markets.
XWNG: The ten standout companies in the space industry, from launch and satellites to the technology supporting them, mostly industrials. It is a concentrated bet on orbit: only ten names carry the fund, so contract wins, launch failures and government budgets swing it hard.
YBST: A basket of GraniteShares YieldBoost funds, each selling options on a different leveraged single-stock product to pay weekly income. It spreads the income strategy across several stocks instead of one: the diversification helps, but every underlying layer still caps gains and adds leverage swings.
YUNG: Companies selling to older consumers: health and wellness, leisure, housing and services for retirees, led by health care and consumer names. It is an actively managed bet on aging demographics: the longevity theme is slow and steady, but the fund depends on one demographic story.
ZCBA: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2030: bonds sold at a discount that return their full face value at maturity, with no interest payments along the way. It is a precise savings target with sharp rate sensitivity: prices swing hard when rates move, then settle at maturity.
ZCBB: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2031: bonds bought at a discount that return full face value at maturity, paying no interest in between. It is a precise long-term savings target: the long wait makes prices very sensitive to interest rates, rising and falling sharply.
ZCBC: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2032: deep-discount bonds that grow to full face value at maturity without paying interest along the way. It is a set-and-forget savings target for a known year: prices swing a lot with rates in the meantime, then converge at maturity.
ZCBE: US Treasury zero-coupon bonds that all come due in 2033, bought at a discount and paying no interest along the way, just full face value at maturity. Held to 2033 the payoff is set, but until then the long wait makes its price swing hard with rates.
